title: U.S. House · California's 38th District
area: Southeast Los Angeles County and San Gabriel Valley, including El Monte, Baldwin Park, West Covina, and Whittier.

context.text: This is an open seat with no incumbent in the race, following California's 2025 congressional redistricting (Proposition 50). California uses a top-two nonpartisan primary; in the June 2, 2026 primary, Hilda Solis (D) placed first with 47.6% and Pedro Casas (R) placed second, advancing to the November general election.

candidates.name: Hilda Solis
candidates.currentRole: Los Angeles County Supervisor, District 1 (2014–2026); did not seek re-election to that seat in 2026

summary.text: Hilda Solis is a Democrat and member of the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors who is running for the newly drawn, open 38th District. Raised in La Puente as the daughter of immigrants, she served on a community college board, in the California Assembly and Senate, and in Congress (2001-2009) before becoming U.S. Secretary of Labor under President Obama (2009-2013). She was elected to the Board of Supervisors in 2014 and did not seek re-election to it in 2026.

background.text: Born in Los Angeles in 1957 and raised in La Puente, California, the daughter of immigrant parents; graduated from La Puente High School in 1975.
Earned a bachelor's degree from California State Polytechnic University, Pomona (1979) and a Master of Public Administration from the University of Southern California (1981).

Worked in the Carter White House Office of Hispanic Affairs and as a management analyst in the civil rights division of the federal Office of Management and Budget; in 1982 she became director of the California Student Opportunity and Access Program.
Was elected to the Rio Hondo Community College District board of trustees in 1985 and re-elected in 1989.

Served in the California State Assembly (1992-1994) and California State Senate (1994-2001); she was the first Hispanic woman to serve in the State Senate and received the John F. Kennedy Library Foundation's Profile in Courage Award in 2000 for her work on environmental justice.
Represented California in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2001 to 2009, in the 31st District (2001-2003) and then the 32nd District (2003-2009).
Served as the 25th U.S. Secretary of Labor under President Barack Obama from February 2009 to January 2013.

Won the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors First District seat outright in June 2014 and took office that December; she served as chair of the board in 2015-2016 and 2020-2021. Her term ends December 7, 2026, and she did not run for re-election to the seat.
According to her campaign website, her work as a supervisor has included the Measure H homelessness funding measure, Project Roomkey, and a $20 million workforce and job training program.

positions.summary: As an L.A. County supervisor, says she has led 14 motions in response to federal immigration raids, including legal action against unlawful arrests and seizures.
positions.quote: since the raids began, I’ve led 14 motions to protect Los Angeles County residents.

record.text: Authored SB 115 (1999), California's first environmental justice law, requiring the state EPA to adopt environmental justice standards; the Senate passed it 23-14 on 1999-05-24 and Governor Gray Davis signed it.

Authored SB 218 (1999), requiring courts to make domestic-violence protective-order forms available in languages other than English; the Senate passed it 26-5 on 1999-05-25 and it was signed into law.
Voted yes on AB 633 (garment-industry wage-theft protections, including joint liability for manufacturers and retailers), which passed the California Senate 24-13 on 1999-09-09.

summary.text: Pedro 'Antonio' Casas is a Republican and retired U.S. Army colonel who is a clinical, forensic, and aero-medical psychologist. Born in El Paso, Texas, he grew up in Baldwin Park and, according to his campaign website, served 29 years in the Army before retiring in September 2023. He is running for the open 38th District seat, describing himself as a native of the district.

background.text: Born in 1962 in El Paso, Texas, to Mexican immigrant parents, and raised in Baldwin Park, California, according to his campaign website; graduated from Don Bosco Technical Institute in 1981.

Earned a Bachelor of Science in psychology from the University of La Verne in 1986 and a Ph.D. in counseling psychology from the University of California, Santa Barbara in 1996, according to his campaign website.
According to his campaign website, served more than 29 years in the U.S. Army, including three deployments to theaters of war, and rose to the rank of Colonel.

His campaign website says his Army assignments included Division Psychologist along the DMZ in South Korea, commanding medical detachments in Iraq and Afghanistan, commanding units in Germany, and serving as chief of behavioral health departments at medical centers in Honolulu and Washington, D.C.; he completed a post-doctoral fellowship in forensic psychology.
Retired from the Army in September 2023, according to his campaign website.
Identifies as Dr. Pedro 'Antonio' Casas, Ph.D., a retired Colonel in the U.S. Army and a clinical, forensic, and aero-medical psychologist.
Says he grew up in the 38th Congressional District, contrasting himself with opponents he describes as not being from the area.
background.quote: As the only candidate, regardless of political party, I originate from the very heart of the 38th Congressional District. Unlike others, I am not an outsider; I understand and can genuinely represent what I have grown up knowing.

priorities.text: Campaign site lists education standards, combating fentanyl trafficking, criminal-justice policy, border security, and addressing inflation and the cost of housing, food, and utilities as priorities, along with tax cuts and reduced business regulation.

positions.summary: Lists barring transgender women from competing against women in sports among his priorities.
positions.quote: Back to basics in sports by restricting biological men from competing against women.

positions.summary: Campaign priorities page lists supporting private school vouchers.
positions.quote: Support the implementation of private school vouchers.

statements.quote: Support law enforcement while opposing any defunding measures.
Address immigration reform, including securing the southern border.

researchNotes: Neither candidate has completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey. No current campaign-issues page or public statements were found for Solis beyond her official biography, so no priorities/positions are cited for her. Her state legislative record (record items above, from official California Legislature roll calls) does not map squarely onto any of the guide's 15 fixed issue statements, so no vote-based positions were added; her extensive prior record as a member of Congress (2001–2009) and Secretary of Labor is not detailed here since it predates the 'record is what an officeholder did in office' scope available from the sources checked. A separately reported 1995-96 minimum-wage bill she championed (vetoed by Gov. Wilson, later enacted by voters as Proposition 210) could not be confirmed to an exact bill number and official roll call within the research budget, so it is not included. Pedro Casas: campaign priorities page (casasforcongress.com/priorities) is the basis for his entries. Biography gaps: Solis's education and early-career details come from Ballotpedia, Wikipedia, and her 2022 campaign page; no current campaign-site biography was loaded. Casas's biography is entirely self-reported on his campaign site, which also contains some outdated references to another district number.
